theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main job of an officer who advises on organisation policy in a public body?
options: To analyse issues and give sound options and advice
To make the final policy decision on the body's behalf
To write every procedure that frontline staff will use
To announce each new policy to the media and public

That the option should be chosen anyway, as it is best

options: That other public agencies already charge similar fees

options: Only the political effects on the governing party

options: Whether the police liked the lights

options: To make the paper look longer

shortAnswers.stem: Laws, taxes, grants and information campaigns are all tools a public body can use to achieve a policy aim. Complete the term: policy ____.
Policies usually pass through stages: agenda setting, formulation, decision, implementation and evaluation. Complete the name for this sequence: the policy ____.
A policy is mainly meant to help or influence certain people, such as tenants in arrears or small vendors. Complete the term for them: target ____.
A policy option costs J$12 million and its benefits are valued at J$30 million. What is its net benefit, in J$ million?
What two-word term names the results of a policy that nobody planned, whether good or bad?
What one word names the fairness of how a policy's costs and benefits fall on different groups, such as rural, poor or elderly people?
Each of 1,500 firms would need about 4 extra hours a year to meet a proposed reporting rule. Valuing their time at J$1,000 an hour, what would the rule cost them in total each year, in J$?
What one-word term names a small-scale trial of a policy in one area before it is introduced more widely?
What two-word term names the statement of what a policy is meant to achieve, against which the options are judged?
Of 240 public submissions on a Green Paper, 84 opposed one proposal. What percentage opposed it?
Policies of different ministries or units should work together rather than against each other. Complete the term: policy ____.
A fee of J$2,000 applies to 6,000 licences a year, and collecting it costs J$1,500,000 a year. What is the net revenue, in J$?
What one-word term names the comparison case that shows what would have happened without the policy, used to judge its real effect?
A programme costs J$9,600,000 and helps 600 people into jobs. What is the cost per job, in J$?
What one word names the policy instrument that requires or forbids behaviour by law, such as a licence requirement or a ban?

essays.stem: The board of a public housing agency asks for policy advice because rent arrears from tenants are rising. Explain how you would define and analyse the problem before you consider any options.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first agree the question with the board: are they worried about lost income, the hardship of tenants, or both? Next I would measure the problem: total arrears, how fast they are rising, the number of tenants in arrears, the size of the debts and where they are, using the agency's rent records for at least three years. I would then look for causes rather than assume them. A problem tree would help, with the effect, rising arrears, at the top and possible causes below: job losses or rising living costs, rents raised faster than incomes, difficult payment methods, weak follow-up by staff, or a belief that arrears are never enforced. I would test each cause with evidence: payment data by method and area, a short survey or interviews with tenants in arrears, staff views, and comparison with other housing bodies. I would also check the legal and policy framework that governs rents and evictions. The result would be a clear problem statement, for example that most new arrears come from tenants paying in cash in rural areas, which then guides which options are worth considering.
markingPoints: Clarifies the question and concern with the board
Measures the size, trend and spread of the problem with records
Uses a structured method such as a problem tree to identify causes
Tests causes with evidence from tenants, staff and comparisons
Ends with a clear, evidence-based problem statement that guides options

essays.stem: Compare regulation, financial incentives and public education as policy instruments for reducing plastic waste in a municipality, and recommend a mix.
essays.modelAnswer: Regulation, such as a by-law banning certain single-use plastics or requiring businesses to separate waste, gives a clear rule and can change behaviour quickly. However, it needs enforcement staff, may be resisted by small businesses and can push problems elsewhere if alternatives are not available. Financial incentives, such as a deposit on bottles, lower fees for households that separate waste or grants for recyclers, work with people's interests and can be popular, but they cost money and need systems to pay and check them. Public education, such as school programmes, radio and community meetings, is cheap per person and builds understanding and support, but on its own it often changes knowledge more than behaviour, and results take time. I would recommend a mix. Start with education and community partners to explain the problem and the change, add incentives such as a bottle deposit and easy collection points so the right behaviour is convenient, and then bring in a targeted regulation, for example on plastic bags, with a clear start date. Monitoring the amount of plastic reaching the dump would show whether the mix works.
markingPoints: Evaluates regulation with strengths and limits
Evaluates financial incentives with strengths and limits
Evaluates public education with strengths and limits
Recommends a sensible sequenced mix
Justifies the mix and includes monitoring of results

essays.stem: A public registry has three options to cut waiting times from 20 days. Option A: more staff, J$30 million a year, cutting the wait to 12 days. Option B: an online system, J$45 million once plus J$5 million a year, cutting the wait to 6 days. Option C: longer opening hours, J$12 million a year, cutting the wait to 16 days. Over five years, compare the total costs and the cost per day of waiting removed, and recommend an option.
essays.modelAnswer: Over five years, Option A costs 5 × J$30 million = J$150 million and removes 8 days (20 − 12), so each day removed costs J$150 million ÷ 8 = J$18.75 million. Option B costs J$45 million + (5 × J$5 million) = J$70 million and removes 14 days (20 − 6), so each day removed costs J$70 million ÷ 14 = J$5 million. Option C costs 5 × J$12 million = J$60 million and removes 4 days (20 − 16), so each day removed costs J$60 million ÷ 4 = J$15 million. Option C has the lowest total cost, but Option B gives by far the biggest cut in waiting and the best value per day removed. I would recommend Option B, but my advice would set out its risks: the system may be late or fail, staff need training, and some customers have poor internet access. To manage these, the agency should keep an assisted counter service and help points in post offices or libraries, and could use part of Option C for a short time while the system is introduced. The advice should also state the assumptions and recommend tracking waiting times monthly.
markingPoints: Calculates five-year costs: A J$150m, B J$70m, C J$60m
Calculates cost per day removed: A J$18.75m, B J$5m, C J$15m
Recognises C is cheapest in total but B gives best value and biggest cut
Recommends B with risks such as delay, training and digital access
Proposes ways to manage risks and to monitor results

essays.stem: A new national policy requires all public agencies to cut their paper use by half within three years. Explain how you would advise your agency's board on what the policy means and how the agency should respond.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first read the national policy and any guidance carefully to set out exactly what it requires: the target, the starting year, what counts as paper use, the reporting duties and any support offered. I would then establish the agency's baseline, for example how many reams it buys, which processes use most paper, and which forms the law requires on paper, so that the board can see the size of the task. Next I would identify the gaps and options: moving forms online, electronic approvals, double-sided printing by default, digital records management and changing rules that require signed paper copies. For each option I would estimate cost, savings, legal issues, the effect on customers who are not online, staff training and ICT needs, and risks such as data security. I would then recommend a phased plan with yearly targets that reach a 50% cut within three years, a named lead and a way of reporting progress. The advice would also point out any conflicts with our own policies or laws that need changing, and where the agency might need help or more time.
markingPoints: Sets out exactly what the national policy requires
Establishes the agency's baseline
Identifies gaps and options to comply
Assesses costs, legal issues, equity, ICT and risks for the options
Recommends a phased, monitored plan and flags conflicts or support needed

essays.stem: Explain the stages of developing a public policy through a Green Paper and a White Paper in Jamaica, and describe how consultation responses should be analysed and used in the advice given to decision-makers.
essays.modelAnswer: A policy issue is first researched and options are developed by the ministry's policy unit, with input from other agencies. The proposals are then set out in a Green Paper, a discussion document approved for release so that the public, interest groups and other bodies can comment within a set period, often through written submissions, meetings in the parishes and online channels. After consultation, the ministry revises the proposals and prepares a White Paper, which sets out the approved policy, before any law or programme follows. Analysing the responses well is central to sound advice. Each submission should be logged, and the comments grouped by proposal and by type of respondent, such as businesses, community groups and individuals. Counting support and opposition helps, but the adviser should weigh the reasons and evidence as well as the numbers, because an organised campaign may send many identical replies. New evidence or practical problems raised should be tested. The advice should then summarise the main views fairly, say how each issue has been dealt with, and explain why some suggestions were not taken up.
markingPoints: Describes research and option development before the Green Paper
Explains the Green Paper as a discussion document with consultation
Explains the White Paper as the approved policy
Describes logging and grouping responses, weighing reasons as well as numbers
Reports views fairly and explains how they were used in the advice

essays.stem: A ministry's policy of giving free school uniforms to needy students has run for five years. Explain how you would evaluate it and advise whether to continue, change or end it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would evaluate the policy against clear questions. Relevance: is there still a real need, for example are families still kept from sending children to school because of uniform costs? Effectiveness: has it met its aims, such as better attendance among students who received uniforms, compared with similar students who did not? Efficiency: what has it cost per student, and could the same result be achieved more cheaply, for example through vouchers with local suppliers rather than central purchase? Equity: are the neediest students reached, including in rural schools, and are some missing out because of how applications work? Sustainability: can the ministry afford it in the coming years? Evidence would come from school attendance records, programme spending, a sample survey of principals and parents, and complaints. I would compare results with the baseline from before the policy. If it meets a real need and works, I would advise continuing it, perhaps with changes to targeting or delivery to reduce cost. If the need has fallen or another programme now covers it, I would advise merging or ending it, with notice to schools and families.
markingPoints: Tests relevance and effectiveness with comparisons
Tests efficiency and considers cheaper delivery
Tests equity and sustainability
Uses suitable evidence sources and the baseline
Gives a reasoned recommendation to continue, change or end, with handling

essays.stem: Explain how an adviser should assess the effect of a policy proposal on different groups, and why this matters, using the example of moving a public service online.
essays.modelAnswer: Moving a service online can cut costs and queues, but its effects will not be the same for everyone. The adviser should first identify the groups who use the service and who might be affected differently: elderly people, people in rural areas with poor internet, people with disabilities, people with low literacy, people without bank cards, and small businesses. She should gather evidence on each group, such as how customers apply now, data on internet access and phone ownership, and the views of community groups and disability organisations. For each group she would consider the likely benefits and harms, for example less travel for young urban users but exclusion for elderly rural users. She should then suggest ways to reduce harm, such as keeping an assisted counter, help points in post offices or libraries, phone support, accessible website design and cash payment options. This matters because public services must be fair and open to all, and the law expects reasonable access, especially for people with disabilities. Ignoring these effects could leave the people most in need without the service and damage trust in the agency.
markingPoints: Identifies the groups who may be affected differently
Gathers evidence on each group, including from their representatives
Weighs likely benefits and harms for each group
Suggests practical measures to reduce harm
Explains why fairness matters for public bodies and trust

essays.stem: A municipal corporation is considering a policy to ban vending on the main street of a busy town. Analyse the possible unintended consequences and explain how your advice would address them.
essays.modelAnswer: The policy aims to ease congestion and improve safety and cleanliness. However, it could have several unintended consequences. Vendors who lose their spot may lose their income, which could cause hardship for families and raise local poverty. They may simply move to side streets or bus stops, moving the congestion rather than removing it, or vend at night, making enforcement harder. Shoppers who buy from vendors may go elsewhere, which could hurt nearby shops too. Conflict between vendors and enforcement officers could increase, with a risk of protests and damage to the corporation's reputation. If enforcement is uneven, the policy could be seen as unfair or open to bribery. My advice would set out these risks with evidence from similar towns. I would recommend consulting vendors and shop owners before any decision, offering a well-located, affordable alternative market or vending zone with basic facilities, phasing the change in with notice, registering vendors, and training officers to enforce fairly. I would also recommend monitoring congestion, side-street vending, complaints and vendors' incomes after the change, so that the policy can be adjusted.
markingPoints: States the policy's aim
Identifies economic and social consequences for vendors and families
Identifies displacement, enforcement and reputational risks
Recommends consultation, an alternative site and phased, fair enforcement
Recommends monitoring so the policy can be adjusted

essays.stem: Explain why a public body's policies need to be coherent with each other and with national policy, and describe how an adviser can find and resolve conflicts between them.
essays.modelAnswer: Policies are coherent when they support each other and the body's mission, and when they fit national policy and the law. Conflicts cause real problems: staff do not know which rule to follow, citizens receive mixed messages, money is wasted when one policy undoes another, and the body may be challenged for acting inconsistently. For example, a ministry might promote rural services while another policy closes rural offices to save money. To find conflicts, an adviser should keep a map of the body's policies and the national policies that affect it, check every new proposal against related policies and laws, and ask other units and agencies whether the proposal affects their work. Regular reviews of the whole policy set help to reveal overlaps and gaps. To resolve a conflict, the adviser should first make it visible to decision-makers, with evidence of its effects. She should then work with the other unit or agency to agree which aim takes priority, or design an option that meets both, such as mobile services instead of full offices. The agreed solution should be recorded and the affected policies updated.
markingPoints: Defines policy coherence, including fit with national policy and law
Explains the problems that conflicts cause, with an example
Describes ways to find conflicts: mapping, checks, consultation, reviews
Describes resolving conflicts with decision-makers and other bodies
Records the agreed solution and updates the policies

essays.stem: The board of a public agency wants to introduce a new performance-based grant for community groups across the island, but the evidence that it will work is limited. Recommend whether and how it should be piloted and evaluated before full adoption, and justify your advice.
essays.modelAnswer: I would recommend a pilot rather than an island-wide launch, because the evidence is weak, the grant involves public money and a poorly designed scheme could be hard to reverse once groups depend on it. The pilot should run for about a year in two or three parishes that differ, for example one urban, one rural and one mixed, so the results show how the scheme works in different conditions. Before it starts, the agency should set clear objectives and measures, such as the number of projects completed and their results for the community, and record a baseline. It would help to compare the pilot parishes with similar parishes that keep the current grant, so that changes can be linked to the new scheme. The evaluation should also look at how fair and easy the application and reporting process is for small groups, the cost of administering it and any risks of misuse. An independent or separate unit should evaluate it. At the end, the advice to the board should recommend adopting, changing or dropping the scheme, based on the evidence. This approach limits risk while allowing innovation.
markingPoints: Recommends a pilot and justifies it by weak evidence and risk to public money
Chooses varied pilot areas and a sensible length
Sets objectives, measures, a baseline and a comparison group
Evaluates fairness, administration cost and misuse risk, ideally independently
Ends with an evidence-based decision to adopt, change or drop

practical1.title: Analyse a policy problem and appraise the policy options
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group an issue pack from a made-up public body, for example rising rent arrears at a housing agency, low use of a new online permit service, or illegal dumping in a parish. The pack contains figures for three years, survey results, short notes of staff and community views, a list of possible options with their costs and expected benefits in J$, and the body's objectives. As a group, analyse the problem and appraise the options. Produce: a problem tree on a flipchart showing causes and effects; a one-page evidence table that rates each source for reliability; a table of at least three options (including keeping the current policy) using different policy instruments, with five-year costs, benefits, net benefit or cost per result, and every sum checked twice; a one-page equity and risk check showing which groups gain or lose and the main risks; and a one-page recommendation to the board that states the preferred option and why. Give each member a named role: lead adviser (keeps time and writes the recommendation), problem analyst (leads the problem tree), evidence officer (prepares the evidence table), options and cost analyst (prepares the options table and figures), and equity and risk officer (prepares the equity and risk check). In a group of four, the lead adviser also prepares the evidence table. At the end, each member explains their part to the assessor in two minutes.
materials: Issue pack and the body's objectives from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
photos: The flipchart with roles and timetable
The problem tree showing causes and effects
The evidence table with reliability ratings
The options table with the second check of the figures marked
The one-page recommendation to the board
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Problem tree separates causes from effects and is based on the pack's evidence
Evidence is rated sensibly for reliability
Options use different instruments and include keeping the current policy
Costs, benefits and comparisons are correct and were checked twice
Equity and risk check names who gains or loses and suggests ways to reduce harm
Recommendation follows from the analysis and is stated clearly with reasons
safety: Use only the made-up public body, names and figures; keep the pack confidential to the group and assessor
Present all evidence fairly, including evidence that does not support the preferred option
Listen to every member's ideas respectfully and share the work fairly
Take short breaks and keep cables and bags out of walkways

practical2.title: Evaluate an existing policy and advise the board on its future
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group an evaluation pack on a policy that a made-up public body has run for several years, for example free bus passes for senior citizens in a parish, a fee waiver for small business permits, or a staff flexible-hours policy. The pack includes the policy's aims, its yearly costs, results for the areas or groups covered, results for a similar area or group not covered, survey findings, complaints and a change in national policy that affects it. As a group: (1) work out the key figures, such as cost per person helped and the change compared with the area not covered, checking every sum twice; (2) judge the policy against relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, equity and sustainability, with evidence for each; (3) agree a recommendation to continue, change or end the policy, with the main implications (financial, legal, staffing and equity); (4) give a 10-minute oral briefing to a board panel played by the assessor and one or two other trainees, using a one-page briefing note or up to four slides, and answer their questions; (5) record the panel's decision and actions. Give each member a named role: lead adviser (opens and gives the recommendation), data analyst (works the figures, checked by another member), evaluation officer (writes the judgement against each criterion), implications officer (sets out the financial, legal, staffing and equity implications), and recorder (prepares the briefing note and records the panel's questions and decision). In a group of four, the lead adviser also sets out the implications. Every member must speak in the briefing or answer a question.
materials: Computers with spreadsheet, word-processing and presentation software, and a printer
photos: The figures worked out, with the second check marked
The judgement against each evaluation criterion, with evidence
The briefing to the board panel in progress (notes and slides only if anyone prefers no photo)
The record of the panel's questions, decision and actions
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Figures are correct, were checked twice and use the comparison area fairly
Each criterion is judged with evidence, not opinion
Recommendation follows from the evaluation and covers the main implications
Spoke clearly and impartially in the briefing or answered a question accurately
Advice notes the effect of the change in national policy
Record shows the decision, actions, owners and dates
safety: Treat the evaluation pack as confidential and use only the made-up names and data
Speak respectfully to the panel and to each other, and disagree with ideas, not people
Ask permission before photographing anyone; photograph notes and slides if a person prefers
Share the workload fairly and take a short break between preparing and briefing
